claims.text: The DFT-based Z method is less computationally expensive than full ab initio thermodynamic integration.
The DFT-based Z method can calculate melting temperature with reasonable accuracy.
Latent heat obtained with the Z method can be used to derive entropy and enthalpy of fusion.
The Z method can determine the volume change at the melting point.
In the proposed Z-method protocol, the system is heated at constant volume until it spontaneously transforms from solid to liquid.
A sufficiently large periodic simulation cell permits metastable heating and nucleation events.
Melting produces an abrupt transition from crystalline atomic order to a disordered liquid structure.
The solid-to-liquid transition is accompanied by a sudden jump in internal energy.
The transition is accompanied by a sudden jump in volume.
Single-phase heating in the Z method produces a characteristic Z-shaped energy-versus-temperature relation.
The energy discontinuity at spontaneous melting reflects the latent heat of fusion.
Energy and volume discontinuities can be used to extract melting temperature and fusion thermodynamics.
The simulation should exhibit a clear energy jump at a specific temperature.
The simulation should exhibit a clear volume jump at a specific temperature.
Z-method estimates should compare favorably with full thermodynamic-integration benchmarks.
Finite simulation-cell size can limit the efficiency or accuracy of the method.
DFT approximations for high-temperature anharmonicity and the choice of simulation parameters can limit the method's accuracy.
The quantitative accuracy of the Z method for entropy and enthalpy of fusion across diverse high-melting materials remains incompletely evaluated.

contradictions.description: The protocol specifies constant-volume simulations, but later asserts and proposes measuring a discontinuous volume jump within those simulations. A fixed-volume trajectory cannot directly display a volume-versus-temperature jump; determining the melting volume change would require additional simulations at different volumes or pressures, or an equation-of-state/free-energy analysis.

The hypothesis treats the energy jump from a constant-volume simulation as latent heat and states that both entropy and enthalpy follow from it. At fixed volume the direct discontinuity is an internal-energy difference, whereas enthalpy also requires the pressure-volume contribution and entropy requires an appropriate transition temperature and thermodynamic relation.
